1016.title: The Warsaw ghetto uprising (1943)
1016.hook: young fighters resist for weeks, beginning on the eve of Passover
1016.howItsDone: Jews remember the Warsaw ghetto uprising on Yom HaShoah, whose full Hebrew name means the day of the Holocaust and of heroism, and some families mention the fighters at their Passover seder.

segments.voice: Yesterday, spiritual resistance, and your line: they kept shabbat. Did you keep one practice of yours on purpose? Today, resistance of another kind, in the same ghetto where the archive was buried. Day one thousand sixteen.

The eve of Passover. Somewhere in the world, families are setting tables, laying out matzah, getting ready to tell the story of slaves who walked out of Egypt. In the Warsaw ghetto, early in the morning, German troops march in through the gates to empty it for good. And from the windows and rooftops above them, someone opens fire. Young Jews, with a few pistols and homemade bombs, are fighting back. Today's word is what began that morning.
screen: `THE EVE OF PASSOVER.` → `TROOPS AT THE GATES.` → `FIRE FROM THE ROOFTOPS.`

segments.voice: By then, the deportations had already swept through the Warsaw ghetto. Those left knew where the trains went. Young men and women from underground groups, some of them from youth movements, had decided that if they were going to die, it would not be quietly. They gathered what weapons they could buy or smuggle. They dug bunkers under the buildings. There were two fighting groups. The larger, the Jewish Fighting Organization, was led by Mordecai Anielewicz, a young man himself; the Jewish Military Union fought alongside it. When the Germans came in on the eve of Passover, the fighters drove them back on the first day. The Germans returned with more troops and began burning the ghetto, building by building, to force people out of hiding. The fighters held out for weeks. Anielewicz died in a bunker with others of his command. Before that, in a letter to a comrade outside the walls, he wrote that his life's dream had come true: he had seen Jewish self-defense in the ghetto with his own eyes. At the end, the German commander blew up the Great Synagogue of Warsaw, to mark that it was over. The fighters did not expect to win. That was never the point. They fought for how the story would end. And it began on Passover, the night that remembers going out from slavery. The Torah says of that night: "And this day shall be unto you for a memorial." Some say families in the bunkers held a seder that night, telling the story of the Exodus while the ghetto burned above them. Israel's day of Holocaust remembrance carries this in its name: the day of the Shoah and of heroism.
screen: `THOSE LEFT KNEW WHERE THE TRAINS WENT.` · `BUNKERS, PISTOLS, HOMEMADE BOMBS.` · `HOLDING OUT FOR WEEKS.` · `THEY FOUGHT FOR HOW IT WOULD END.` · then, large: `THIS DAY SHALL BE UNTO YOU FOR A MEMORIAL.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: honor one act of courage. Sit, and let your breath slow. Bring to mind an act of courage you have seen up close. Someone who told the truth when it cost them. Someone who stood up for a person being mocked. Someone who kept going through an illness, or walked into a hard conversation. It doesn't need to be large. Hold that person in mind, and let yourself honor what they did. Then decide how you'll honor it today: tell them, or tell someone else about them. The bell holds the time.
The Warsaw ghetto uprising. Young Jewish fighters, beginning on the eve of Passover, who held out against the German army for weeks so the story would not end quietly. Today's word.
Your line: they fought. Today, name one person's courage out loud, to them or to someone else. Day one thousand sixteen.

1017.title: The Righteous
1017.hook: non-Jews who risked their lives to hide and save Jews
1017.howItsDone: Jewish communities honor rescuers through Yad Vashem's title Righteous Among the Nations, with trees and names at the memorial in Jerusalem; some families stay in touch with the families of those who hid them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Warsaw ghetto uprising, and your line: they fought. Which act of courage did you stop to honor? Today, courage of another kind, from people on the other side of the walls. Day one thousand seventeen.

A tree on a hillside in Jerusalem, with a small plaque at its foot. On the plaque, a name that isn't Jewish. A farmer's name, perhaps, or a nun's, or a diplomat's. Walk a little further and there's another tree, and another name. Each one marks a person who was not Jewish, who lived through the Nazi years, and who hid a Jewish neighbor in an attic, forged a paper, or opened a door when opening it could have cost everything. Some of them were caught. Some of them were never thanked in their lifetimes. Today's word is the title they were given.
screen: `A TREE ON A HILLSIDE.` → `A NAME THAT ISN'T JEWISH.` → `A DOOR THAT COULD COST EVERYTHING.`

segments.voice: Yad Vashem, Israel's Holocaust memorial, gives these people a title: Righteous Among the Nations. In Hebrew, chasidei umot ha-olam. The idea behind it is much older than the war. A rabbinic teaching recorded in the Tosefta says that the righteous of the nations of the world have a share in the world to come. Goodness, in that teaching, doesn't belong to one people. The stories are as different as the people in them. A pastor and his wife, André and Magda Trocmé, in the French village of Le Chambon-sur-Lignon, where villagers took in Jewish children and refugees. A Japanese diplomat in Lithuania, Chiune Sugihara, who kept writing transit visas after his government had said no. A social worker in Warsaw, Irena Sendler, who helped smuggle children out of the ghetto. And people whose names are known only to the families they hid, or to no one at all. Asked later why they did it, some rescuers gave answers so plain they sound almost like a shrug. Someone knocked. You open the door. The book of Proverbs asks the same thing of its reader: rescue those who are being dragged toward death, and don't hold back. And it adds that no one can excuse themselves by saying they didn't know. Remembering the righteous doesn't soften the history around them. It shows something harder: that even then, a person could still choose.
screen: `RIGHTEOUS AMONG THE NATIONS.` · `A VILLAGE, A DIPLOMAT, A SOCIAL WORKER.` · `SOMEONE KNOCKED. YOU OPEN THE DOOR.` · `RESCUE THOSE DRAGGED TOWARD DEATH.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: thank someone who took a risk for you. Settle into your seat and let the breath slow. Bring to mind one person who once took a risk on your behalf. Small counts. A teacher who stood up for you. A friend who told you a hard truth. A stranger who stopped when others walked past. Let their face come clear. Notice what the risk might have cost them. If you pray, you can give thanks for them in the words of your own tradition. If you don't, simply hold them in mind with gratitude. The bell holds the time.
The Righteous. In full, the Righteous Among the Nations: people who were not Jewish and risked their lives to hide and save Jews. Today's word.
Your line: the righteous. Today, send one short message of thanks to the person you thought of, the one who took a risk for you. Day one thousand seventeen.

1018.title: Hannah Senesh
1018.hook: a young poet and paratrooper who went back into occupied Europe
1018.howItsDone: Hannah Senesh's poems are read and sung in Israel, especially Eli, Eli (A Walk to Caesarea) and the match poem, and she is remembered at memorial gatherings and in schools.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the righteous: people outside the walls who opened their doors. Did you thank someone who once took a risk for you? Today, a young woman who went back toward the fire. Day one thousand eighteen.

A beach at Caesarea, on the coast of the land of Israel. A young woman who grew up in Budapest walks along the sand and writes a short poem. In it, she asks that some things never end: the sand and the sea, the rustle of the water, the lightning of the sky, the prayer of a human being. Set to music, it's sung in Israel under the name Eli, Eli. My God, my God. Its title calls it a walk to Caesarea. Not long after, she volunteered to go back into the war that had swallowed her family's Europe. Today, Hannah Senesh.
screen: `A BEACH AT CAESAREA.` → `THE SAND AND THE SEA.` → `SHE WENT BACK.`

segments.voice: Hannah Senesh grew up in a Jewish family in Budapest. She wrote poems and kept a diary from girlhood. As a young woman she moved to the land of Israel, and lived on a kibbutz by the sea called Sdot Yam. Then the news from Europe grew darker. She joined a small group of Jewish volunteers from the land, trained by the British army, who parachuted into occupied Europe. Their mission was to help the Allies, and to reach Jews wherever they could. She came down in Yugoslavia and crossed toward Hungary, where her mother still lived. She was captured at the border. In prison she was beaten and questioned, and the story told about her is that she would not give up her radio code. Her mother, arrested too, saw her there. Hannah was tried and shot by a firing squad, still a young woman. Before she crossed the border, she handed a fellow volunteer a short poem. In it she blesses a match: a match that is used up in lighting a flame. She blesses the flame, and a heart that knows when to stop beating, for the sake of honor. That's a paraphrase; the Hebrew is spare and plain. Notice where she begins and ends. Not with the fire. With the match. A match has one job. It burns itself out so that something else can catch. Some remember her as a fighter. Some remember her first as a poet. Some find both in the same few lines: the walk on the beach, and the match.
screen: `BUDAPEST, A DIARY, A KIBBUTZ BY THE SEA.` · `A PARACHUTE BACK INTO EUROPE.` · `CAPTURED, AND SILENT.` · `BLESSED IS THE MATCH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read one of her lines. Sit, and let your breath settle. Take the beach poem, in paraphrase, one piece at a time. The sand and the sea. The rustle of the water. The lightning of the sky. The prayer of a human being. Say each one slowly, in your head or out loud, and leave a whole breath between them. Then rest on the last one. If you pray, you can let her words carry your prayer for a while. If you don't, let them be a short list of things you'd like never to end. The bell holds the time.
Hannah Senesh. A poet from Budapest who lived by the sea in the land of Israel, and parachuted back into occupied Europe during the war. Today's word.

Your line: the match that kindles. Today, do one small thing that lights something for someone else, even if it costs you a little. And if you'd like, find one of her poems and read it in full. Day one thousand eighteen.

1019.title: Liberation (1945)
1019.hook: the camps are liberated, and survivors face a world that is gone
1019.howItsDone: Jewish communities remember the liberation of the camps on Yom HaShoah and at memorial services, and some survivors and their families mark the day their own camp was liberated.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hannah Senesh, and your line: the match that kindles. What did you light for someone else? Today, the gates open. Go gently with this one. Day one thousand nineteen.

Soldiers push open a gate. They came to fight a war, and nothing prepared them for what's inside: people too thin to stand, barracks full of the sick, a silence that doesn't sound like peace. On the other side of the gate, a prisoner hears that the guards are gone. Free. And almost at once, a second question arrives behind the first. Free to go where? To whom? Is anyone left? Today's word is the first half of that moment. We'll hold the second half too.
screen: `A GATE PUSHED OPEN.` → `FREE.` → `FREE TO GO WHERE?`

segments.voice: As the Allied armies crossed Europe, they reached the camps one after another. Soviet soldiers in the east, at places like Majdanek and Auschwitz. American and British soldiers in the west, at Buchenwald, Dachau, Bergen-Belsen. What they found, they photographed and filmed, and commanders ordered it recorded, so that no one could later say it hadn't happened. Liberation did not end the suffering at once. Soldiers handed out their own rations out of plain kindness: chocolate, tinned meat. But starving bodies could not take rich food, and some who had lived to see the gates open died in the days after. Doctors and nurses learned to feed people slowly. Then came the second question. Survivors went looking for family. They read lists, posted lists, wrote names on walls, asked every stranger from their town. Some walked back home to find no one waiting and strangers living in their houses. And yet, in the middle of all this, something else. At Bergen-Belsen, in the days after the British arrived, a Jewish army chaplain led a Sabbath service among the barracks. Survivors sang, and their voices were recorded. A psalm describes a return from exile in just this strange way: "When the LORD brought back those that returned to Zion, we were like unto them that dream." For those who lived it, liberation could feel like that. Real, and not yet believable. The word means being set free. It doesn't mean being made whole. Both are part of the story.
screen: `THE GATES OPEN.` · `FREED, BUT NOT YET SAFE.` · `NAMES ON LISTS, NAMES ON WALLS.` · `LIKE UNTO THEM THAT DREAM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: think of the survivors. Sit, and let your breath find its own pace. You don't need any picture of the camps. Instead, think of one survivor walking out through a gate, and the first ordinary things that came after. A bowl of soup. A clean shirt. A letter. A name found on a list. Hold that person gently, whoever they were. If you know a survivor's name, or a family story, bring it in. If you pray, you can pray for the survivors and for those who carry their memory. If you don't, simply keep them company in your mind. The bell holds the time.
Liberation. Being set free: the opening of the camps as the war in Europe ended, and the first slow steps of the people inside. Today's word.
Your line: liberation. Today, notice one freedom you have that someone once had to fight for, and don't hurry past it. Day one thousand nineteen.

1020.title: Witness
1020.hook: survivors rebuilt lives and told what happened
1020.howItsDone: Jewish schools, museums and communities invite survivors into classrooms and memorial gatherings, and play recorded testimonies there too, especially around Yom HaShoah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, liberation: set free, but not yet made whole. Which freedom did you stop to notice? Today, what survivors did with the years they were given. Day one thousand twenty.

What do you do with something you saw that the world would rather not hear? Some survivors said that after the war, the people around them changed the subject. So they did the next thing. They married. They worked. They raised children, learned new languages, opened shops in cities they'd never heard of as children. And some of them, sometimes many years later, sat down in front of a microphone, or a classroom, or a camera, and began to say what happened. Slowly. With names. Today's word is what they became.
screen: `A STORY NOBODY WANTED TO HEAR.` → `A NEW LIFE FIRST.` → `THEN, A MICROPHONE.`

segments.voice: In Hebrew, a witness is an ed. The Torah takes witnesses seriously. Leviticus says that someone who has seen or known a thing, and is called to testify, and stays silent, carries the guilt. To have seen is to owe something. And the prophet Isaiah turns a whole people into witnesses. God says: "Ye are My witnesses, saith the LORD." In Hebrew, atem edai. The survivors took up that word in their own way. They wrote memoirs and kept the diaries they'd hidden. They spoke in courtrooms: at the trial of Adolf Eichmann in Jerusalem, survivors took the stand one after another and told the court what they'd lived through. They sat for recorded interviews, now kept in archives like those at Yad Vashem, the USC Shoah Foundation and Yale's Fortunoff archive. Being a witness cost something. Every telling meant going back. Some survivors could never speak of it at all, and their silence is part of the record too. Elie Wiesel, a survivor and writer, put the next step this way: whoever listens to a witness becomes a witness. The survivors will not always be here to speak. But their words are. And whoever hears them carries something forward. The listening is the next link.
screen: `ED: ONE WHO SAW, AND TELLS.` · `YE ARE MY WITNESSES.` · `BOOKS, COURTROOMS, CAMERAS.` · `THE LISTENER BECOMES A WITNESS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: get ready to listen to one survivor's testimony. Sit, and close your eyes if that's comfortable. For now, just listen to the sounds around you: the room, the street, your own breath. Listen the way you'd listen to someone telling you something that matters. Not to fix it. Not to answer it. Only to receive it. If you pray, you can ask for an open ear. If you don't, simply practice the listening itself. Then, later today, find one recorded testimony and give it your whole attention, even for a few minutes. The bell holds the time.
Witness. In Hebrew, ed: someone who saw, and tells. Survivors who told what happened became witnesses for everyone who came after. Today's word.
Your line: witness. Today, listen to one survivor's testimony, a few minutes, with nothing else open on your screen. Day one thousand twenty.

1021.title: Faith after
1021.hook: some survivors lost faith, some kept it, some argued with God; all are honored
1021.howItsDone: Jewish communities hold a wide range of responses to the Holocaust side by side; on Yom HaShoah, memorial services may include psalms, the memorial prayer and Kaddish, and also readings of doubt and protest.

segments.voice: Yesterday, witness: whoever listens to a witness becomes one. Did you hear a survivor's voice? Today, a question some of them carried out of the camps, about God. Day one thousand twenty-one.

Elie Wiesel told a story from the camp where he was held. A few prisoners, learned men, decided to put God on trial. They argued the case through the nights, like a court. At the end, they reached a verdict: guilty. And then, the story goes, one of them looked up and said it was time for the evening prayer. And they prayed. Hold both halves of that story at once. The verdict, and the prayer. Today, faith after.
screen: `GOD ON TRIAL.` → `THE VERDICT: GUILTY.` → `THEN, EVENING PRAYER.`

segments.voice: Survivors came out of the Holocaust with faith in very different shapes. Some lost it. They had prayed, and the prayers seemed to meet nothing, and they could not go back. That answer is honored. Some kept it. They rebuilt synagogues, said Kaddish for their parents, taught their children the blessings over bread and candles. That answer is honored. And some argued. They kept speaking to God, and the speaking was a fight. That third way has deep roots in the Tanakh. When Abraham hears that Sodom will be destroyed, he argues with God to God's face: "Shall not the Judge of all the earth do justly?" The psalmist, feeling abandoned, shouts upward: "Awake, why sleepest Thou, O Lord?" Job argues his case at length, and at the end God says that Job has spoken rightly, and his comforters have not. In this tradition, arguing with God can itself be a kind of prayer. After the war, Jewish thinkers offered many answers, and none of them won. Some reached for an old phrase from Deuteronomy, hester panim, God hiding the face. Some said there is no answer, and that building one would wrong the dead. Some said the only answer was to go on living as Jews, so the story would not end there. This path doesn't pick among them. The person who stopped praying, the one who never stopped, the one who prayed through clenched teeth: each one is honored, and none of them is ours to judge.
screen: `SOME LOST FAITH.` · `SOME KEPT IT.` · `SOME ARGUED WITH GOD.` · `EVERY ANSWER IS HONORED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold one question without answering it. Sit, and let the breath slow. Bring up one question you carry that has no tidy answer. It might be about suffering, or about God, or about someone you lost. Don't try to solve it. Hold it the way you'd hold something heavy that isn't yours to set down yet. When your mind races toward an answer, come back to the question itself. If you pray, you can bring the question to God just as it is, argument and all. If you don't, let it sit beside you in the quiet. The bell holds the time.
Faith after. What survivors did with faith after the Holocaust: some lost it, some kept it, some argued with God. Today's word.
Your line: every answer is honored. Today, when someone tells you how they believe, or don't, listen all the way through without correcting them. Day one thousand twenty-one.

screen: `DAY 1021 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: EVERY ONE HAD A NAME.`

1022.title: Every one had a name
1022.hook: Yad Vashem gathers the name of every victim it can
1022.howItsDone: On Yom HaShoah, communities in Israel and elsewhere hold name-reading ceremonies, and families fill in Pages of Testimony at Yad Vashem for relatives who were murdered.

segments.voice: Yesterday, faith after, and your line: every answer is honored. Did you listen to someone without correcting them? Today the week comes to rest, on names. Day one thousand twenty-two.

On Yom HaShoah, Israel's day of Holocaust remembrance, people step up to microphones in the Knesset, in schools, in synagogues, and read names aloud. One name. Then another. Then the next. A grandmother. A cousin no one else remembers. A child. Sometimes a reader adds a town, or a word about who the person was. The reading doesn't summarize. It doesn't round anything off. It just keeps going, one person at a time. Today's line is the idea underneath that reading.
screen: `NAMES READ ALOUD.` → `ONE, THEN ANOTHER.` → `NOTHING ROUNDED OFF.`

segments.voice: Israel's Holocaust memorial takes its name from the prophet Isaiah. There, God speaks to people who feared they would leave no children to carry their name, and promises them, in the Hebrew, a yad vashem: a monument and a memorial, literally a hand and a name. The same verse goes on: "I will give them an everlasting name, that shall not be cut off." Yad Vashem has spent its life gathering names. One of its tools is plain: the Page of Testimony. A single sheet for a single person. A relative or a friend writes down a name, a town, the names of parents, a job, what is known about how they died, and sometimes attaches a photograph. The pages are kept in the Hall of Names, and the gathering goes on, because some names are still missing. The Israeli poet Zelda wrote a poem about this, in paraphrase: every person has a name, given by God, by parents, by the way they stood and smiled, by the work they did, by the people who loved them. The name-reading ceremonies take their title from it. Now look back at this week. Fighters in the Warsaw ghetto. The Trocmés, Chiune Sugihara, Irena Sendler. Hannah Senesh. Soldiers at the gates, and the people they found. Witnesses who told. Survivors who prayed, or argued, or stopped. All of it comes down, in the end, to persons. Not a number. Each one had a name.
screen: `A HAND AND A NAME.` · `AN EVERLASTING NAME.` · `ONE PAGE FOR ONE PERSON.` · `EVERY ONE HAD A NAME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read one name aloud. Choose one. It might be a name from this week, like Hannah Senesh or Irena Sendler. It might be someone from your own family. Say it out loud, slowly, once. Then sit with it. Not a statistic, not a category. A person who answered to that name when someone called it across a room. If you pray, you can hold that name in your prayer. If you don't, just let it stay in the air of the room with you. Later, if you'd like, look up one name in Yad Vashem's online database. The bell holds the time.
Every one had a name. Each person murdered in the Holocaust was someone, with a name, and the work of remembering gathers them one by one. Today's word.
screen: `EVERY ONE HAD A NAME — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: every one had a name. Today, learn one name and one detail about one person who was lost, and say both out loud. Day one thousand twenty-two.

a monument and a memorial, literally a hand and a name, and an everlasting name.
every victim's name has already been found
the gathering goes on, because some names are still missing.
a Page of Testimony records one person
a name, a town, parents, a job, and what is known, filled in by a relative or friend.

fork.setup: you're asked to fill in a Page of Testimony for a great-aunt. you know only her first name and her town. what do you do?
options: leave it, since you don't know enough.
fork.reveal: pages are filled in by relatives and friends with what they know. a name and a town keep a person from being lost.

original.note: Hebrew: a hand and a name. in Isaiah, a monument and a memorial.

trapdoor: what you thought: Yad Vashem is just the name of a museum.
what it means: a promise that no one is reduced to a number: a page, a name, a reading aloud.
what a scholar hears: Isaiah 56:5, where yad vashem is promised to people who feared no children would carry their name.

sources.ref: Every Man Has a Name (Lekhol ish yesh shem)
